en: The Questions of Milinda:
The Chapter on Vessantara, Concerning the Question of Inference.
6. The Question on Untimely Death “Venerable Nāgasena, as for those beings who die, do they all die only at the proper time, or do they also die prematurely?
“There is, Great King, death at the proper time, and there is also death prematurely.”
“Venerable Nāgasena, who die at the proper time, and who die at the improper time?
“But have you ever seen, Great King, mango trees or rose-apple trees, or other fruit-bearing trees, with fruits falling from them—both unripe and ripe?
“Yes, venerable sir.”
“Great King, as for those fruits that fall from a tree, do they all fall at the proper time, or do some fall even out of season?
“Venerable Nāgasena, those fruits that fall when fully ripe and overripe, all of them fall at the proper time.
But as for the remaining fruits, among them some fall pierced by worms, and some fall struck by a club.”
“Some fall [prematurely], some fall struck by the wind, and some fall having become rotten within;
all of them fall out of season.

“In the same way, Great King, those who die struck by the force of old age die at their proper time; the rest—some die obstructed by karma, some die obstructed by destiny, and some die obstructed by action.”

“Venerable Nāgasena, those who die hindered by karma, those who die hindered by their destination, those who die hindered by their actions, and those who die hindered by the force of old age—all of them die only at the proper time.
Even one who dies while still in the mother’s womb, that is his time; he dies only at the proper time.”
“Even one who dies in the house where he was born—this is his time; he too dies only at his appointed time. Even one who dies in the first month...

[and so on] ...even one who dies at a hundred years of age—this is his time; he dies only at his appointed time. Therefore, venerable Nāgasena, there is no such thing as untimely death; whoever dies, all of them die only at their appointed time.”
“Great King, there are these seven who die prematurely even though their life span is still remaining.
Which seven?
One who is hungry, Great King, not obtaining food, dies prematurely even though his life span is still remaining, with his internal organs destroyed.
One who is thirsty, O Great King, not obtaining water, with a parched heart, dies prematurely even though a further lifespan remains;
one who is bitten by a snake, O Great King, overcome by the force of the venom, not obtaining a physician, dies prematurely even though a further lifespan remains;
one who has consumed poison, O Great King, while his limbs and members are burning, not obtaining an antidote, dies prematurely even though a further lifespan remains.
“Great king, one who has fallen into fire, while burning and unable to find extinction, dies prematurely even though his life span is still remaining;
great king, one who has fallen into water, unable to find a firm footing, dies prematurely even though his life span is still remaining;
great king, one struck by a weapon, being afflicted and unable to find a physician, dies prematurely even though his life span is still remaining.”
"These, O Great King, are the seven who die prematurely even though their life-span is still remaining.
Regarding this, O Great King, I speak with absolute certainty.
There are, O Great King, eight ways in which the death of beings occurs: through that arising from wind, and through that arising from bile."

“Great King, the passing away of beings occurs through [diseases] arising from phlegm, from a combination of humors, from changes in the seasons, from irregular lifestyle, from external injury, and from the ripening of kamma.
In that regard, Great King, that which is passing away due to the ripening of kamma is what is called ‘timely passing away’; the remainder is ‘untimely passing away.’”
And it is said:
“By hunger, by thirst,
by snakebite, and by poison;”
By the power of those who seize him,
he dies there untimely;
by wind, bile, or phlegm.
“By the combination of humors,
by irregularities, by poisons, or by acts of violence,
one dies there prematurely.”
"Great King, some beings die through the ripening of various unwholesome kamma performed in the past. In this case, Great King,
one who previously caused others to die of hunger suffers from hunger for many hundreds of thousands of years—
emaciated, exhausted, with a heart parched and withered, famished, utterly dried up, and burning within."
Being scorched by thirst, he dies—whether young, middle-aged, or old; this too is his timely death.
Furthermore, he who previously caused others to die of thirst becomes a hungry ghost (*preta*) for many hundreds of thousands of years;
being consumed by parching thirst, emaciated, lean, and with a withered heart, he dies of thirst himself—whether young, middle-aged, or old.
This too is his timely death.
He who previously causes others to be bitten by snakes and then kills them will, for many hundreds of thousands of years, roll from the mouth of one python into the mouth of another,
and from the mouth of one black snake into the mouth of another, being devoured by them as they eat.
Just as one bitten by snakes dies— whether young, middle-aged, or old— this too is his timely death. Furthermore,

he who previously causes others to die by administering poison dies himself from that very poison— whether young, middle-aged, or old— with his limbs and members burning for many hundreds of thousands of years,
his body breaking apart and emitting the stench of a corpse.
This too is his timely death.
He who previously causes others to die by fire, after wandering for many hundreds of thousands of years through the realm of Yama as if through a mountain of glowing embers and back again,
with his limbs utterly scorched, dies by fire even while still young.
Whether he be young, middle-aged, or old, this too is his timely death.

He who previously kills others with water dies himself by water—whether he be young, middle-aged, or old—with his limbs wounded, mangled, broken, and weakened, and his mind agitated; this too is his timely death.

“He who previously kills others with a spear dies himself by that very spear—mangled, shattered, crushed, and pierced by the mouth of the spear—for many hundreds of thousands of years, whether he be young, middle-aged, or old; this too is his timely death.
“Venerable Nāgasena, regarding what you say—that there is such a thing as untimely death—pray, point out the reason for this to me.”

“Just as, Great King, a vast mass of fire that has consumed grass, wood, branches, and foliage, having exhausted its fuel, goes out through the depletion of its substrate, and that fire is said to be ‘without calamity, without disaster, extinguished at the proper time’;

even so, Great King, whoever, having lived for many thousands of days, dies worn out by old age through the exhaustion of his lifespan, being without calamity or disaster, he is said to have ‘met death at the proper time.’”
"Or again, great king, suppose there were a vast mass of fire that had consumed grass,
wood, branches, and foliage, and while that grass, wood, branches, and foliage were not yet entirely exhausted, a great rain cloud poured down and extinguished it.
Would that vast mass of fire, great king, be said to have been extinguished at that time?"
“No indeed, Bhante.
“But why, Great King, did that last mass of fire not have the same destination as the first mass of fire?
“Because it was overwhelmed by an incoming cloud of rain, Bhante, that mass of fire was extinguished out of season.”
“In the same way, Great King, whoever dies prematurely does so being oppressed by a sudden illness—
whether arising from wind, or arising from bile, or arising from phlegm, or from a combination of these, or from a change in the seasons, or from an improper lifestyle,
or from injury, or from hunger, or from thirst, or from being bitten by a snake.”
Or one dies prematurely, being oppressed by the force of a disease, or by fire, or by water, or by the impact of a weapon.
This, O Great King, is the reason why premature death exists.

Or again, O Great King, just as when a vast and mighty cloud arises in the sky and rains down, filling both the lowlands and the highlands, it is said: "The rain-cloud pours forth without harm or calamity."

“In the same way, Great King, whoever has lived for a long time and, worn out by old age, dies at the exhaustion of his lifespan without calamity or misfortune, he is said to have ‘met death at the proper time.

Or again, Great King, suppose a very great cloud were to arise in the sky and, before reaching its destination, be dispersed by a mighty wind; would that great cloud, Great King, be said to have ‘vanished at the proper time’?
“No indeed, Bhante.”
“But why, Great King, did that last cloud not have the same speed as the first cloud?
“Because, venerable sir, it was oppressed by a sudden wind; that cloud vanished before it had even reached its time.
“In the very same way, Great King, whoever dies untimely is oppressed by a sudden illness, whether arising from wind... [and so on]...”
Or, oppressed by the force of passion (*sattiva*), one dies prematurely.
This, Great King, is the reason why premature death exists.
Or again, Great King, just as if a powerful, enraged venomous snake were to bite some man—of him...
That poison, being free from calamity and free from misfortune, would bring about death; that poison is called "free from calamity, free from misfortune, having reached its limit.

In the same way, Great King, whoever, having lived for a long time, dies worn out by old age at the exhaustion of his lifespan—being free from calamity and free from misfortune—is called "one free from calamity, free from misfortune, having reached the limit of life, having arrived at timely death."

“Or again, great king, suppose a snake charmer were to give an antidote to one who had been bitten by a powerful venomous snake, thereby rendering the poison harmless even while it was still within him. Would that poison, great king, be said to have vanished at that moment?
“No indeed, venerable sir.
“But why, great king, would that later poison not have gone to the same destination as the earlier poison?”
“Venerable sir, when poison is suppressed by an imported antidote, it is eliminated even before it has reached its target.
“In the same way, great king, whoever dies prematurely does so because they are oppressed by an adventitious disease—whether arising from wind, or [as the text continues]...
or oppressed by the force of a living being’s energy.”
This, O Great King, is the reason why there is such a thing as untimely death.

Or again, O Great King, suppose an archer were to shoot an arrow, and that arrow were to go right to the very end of its path; that arrow would be called "free from danger, free from calamity, having gone to the very end of its path.

In the same way, O Great King, whoever lives for a long time and, worn out by old age, dies at the exhaustion of his lifespan—being free from danger and free from calamity—is said to have "approached death in due season, free from danger and free from calamity."

“Or again, great king, suppose an archer were to shoot an arrow, and someone were to catch that arrow at that very moment—would that arrow, great king, be said to have reached the end of its course and path?
“No, venerable sir.
“But why, great king, would that subsequent arrow not have the same course as the first arrow?”
“Venerable sir, the flow of that stream was interrupted by an external obstruction.
“In the same way, great king, whoever dies prematurely does so because they are oppressed by an adventitious disease— whether arising from wind, or [as detailed in the full passage],
or oppressed by the force of a fever— and thus dies prematurely.”
This, Great King, is the reason why untimely death exists.
Or again, Great King, just as when anyone strikes a vessel made of iron, the sound produced by that striking travels along its path until it reaches its destination;
that sound is said to be "without calamity and without distress."
"Just as one who has reached the very limit of the path leading to whatever destination he has come from," so too,

Great King, whoever, having lived for many thousands of days, dies worn out by old age at the exhaustion of his lifespan, free from calamity and free from distress— he is called "one who has met death at the proper time,
free from calamity and free from distress. Or again, Great King, just as when someone strikes an iron vessel, there is a sound produced by that striking...

“Suppose, great king, a sound were produced, and while the sound had not yet gone far, someone were to touch it; would that sound, at the very moment of being touched, be said to have reached the end of its path of travel?
“Certainly not, venerable sir.”
“But why, Great King, did the final sound not have the same destination as the preceding sound?
“Because, venerable sir, that sound was brought to an end by an adventitious touch.
“In the same way, Great King, whoever dies untimely does so because they are oppressed by an adventitious disease, whether arising from wind... [and so forth].”
Or, oppressed by the force of a [violent] temperament, one dies prematurely.
This, Great King, is the reason why there is death at an untimely time.
Or again, Great King, just as a grain seed that has grown well in a field, when the rain falls properly—
When a field, having been overspread, strewn, and filled with abundant fruit, reaches the time for harvest, that grain is said to be "free from calamity,
free from misfortune, and arrived at its proper season. In the same way, Great King,

whoever lives for many thousands of days and, worn out by old age, dies at the exhaustion of his lifespan without calamity or misfortune, he is said to have "approached death at the proper season, free from calamity and free from misfortune."
"Or again, great king, suppose a grain seed that has grown well in a field were to perish due to a lack of water; would that grain, great king, be called 'seasonally matured'?
"No, venerable sir.
"But why, great king, would that later grain not have the same destination as the earlier grain?"
“Venerable sir, that grain has died because it was afflicted by an external heat.
“In the same way, great king, whoever dies prematurely does so because they are afflicted by an adventitious disease—whether arising from wind, or...
or afflicted by the force of poison—they die prematurely.”
“This, O Great King, is the reason why premature death exists.
Have you not previously heard, O Great King, that when worms arise in a field of perfectly ripe young grain, they destroy it along with its roots?
“I have indeed heard this, venerable sir, and I have seen it myself.”
“Great King, was that crop lost in its proper season, or was it lost out of season?
“Out of season, venerable sir. For if those worms had not eaten that crop, venerable sir, it would have reached the time for harvesting.
“But, Great King, does a crop perish through external damage, or does an undamaged crop reach the time for harvesting?”
“Yes, venerable sir.
“In the same way, great king, whoever dies untimely does so either oppressed by a sudden disease, or by one arising from wind … [and so on] … or oppressed by the force of a poison.”
“This, great king, is the reason why there is untimely death.

Have you not heard before, great king, that when a crop has ripened, bent down by the weight of its fruit, and the leaves are covered in clusters, a certain kind of rain called a *karakavassa* falls and destroys it, rendering it fruitless?
“I have heard this before, venerable sir, and I have seen it myself.”
“Great King, was that crop destroyed in its proper season, or was it destroyed out of season?
“Out of season, Bhante. For if that crop had not been rained upon by the rain of the clouds at the time of harvest, it would have reached the time for harvesting.
“But, Great King, does the crop perish through an external injury, or does a crop free from injury reach the time for harvesting?”
“Yes, venerable sir,” he replied. “In the same way, great king, whoever dies prematurely does so because they are oppressed by a sudden illness—
whether arising from wind, or arising from bile, or arising from phlegm, or from a combination of these, or from changes in the weather.”
Or, oppressed by what arises from avoiding uneven ground, or by self-inflicted injury, or by hunger, or by thirst,
or by being bitten by a snake, or by sitting on uneven terrain, or by fire, or by water, or by the force of a weapon, one dies prematurely. However,
if one were not oppressed by an adventitious disease, one would reach death at the proper time.
“This, O Great King, is the reason why there is untimely death.
“It is wonderful, venerable Nāgasena! It is marvelous, venerable Nāgasena! Well shown is the reason, well shown is the simile for the illustration of untimely death;
it has been made clear and manifest that ‘there is untimely death.’”

"It has been explained, it has been made clear; even a mindless person, venerable Nāgasena, would reach a conclusion from even a single simile that 'there is untimely death,' how much more so a conscious human being?
By the very first simile, venerable sir, I was convinced that 'there is untimely death'; yet, desiring to hear further clarifications, I did not accept [the matter as finished]."
The sixth question: On Untimely Death.
